I2.quote: Here, it is seen that the pure carbon spheres adsorb small amount of H2, whereas modification of DMHCS with Pd nanoparticles leads to a significant increase of the H2 uptake

I3.quote: Fig. 8A shows the H2 sorption isotherms of the pristine and doped DMHCS spheres at 40 °C up to 45 bar. [...] the H2 uptake capacities at 45 bar are 0.17 [...] wt% for DMHCS
I3.location: main, p. 6 (journal p. 30466), Results and discussion; Fig. 8A (p. 7)

I4.quote: Table 2 shows the parameters such as BET surface areas [...] The surface area decreased from 1378 for DMHCS to 573 (Pd@C_24), 282 (2-Pd@C_24), 166 (3-Pd@C_24) and 564 m2/g.
I4.location: main, p. 6 (journal p. 30466), Results and discussion; Table 2

I5.quote: A disordered mesoporous hollow carbon spheres were decorated with Pd nanoparticles and their H2 sorption performance was examined at 40 °C and up to 45 bar.

notes: Volumetric (Sieverts) H2 uptake at 40 °C (313.15 K) to 45 bar on pristine DMHCS and four Pd-loaded DMHCS samples; values in text, Table 3 (20 and 30 bar) and Fig. 8A/B. The pristine DMHCS is a carbon sorbent (TGA: 'The residual weight after complete oxidation of carbon spheres was 0 wt%', p. 5), as are Pd@C_24 (30 wt% Pd) and Pd@C_72 (34 wt% Pd); 2-Pd@C_24 (59 wt%) and 3-Pd@C_24 (75 wt% Pd) are Pd-majority by mass and so not carbon sorbents under §3. BET areas measured by N2 at 77 K (Micromeritics ASAP 2010 M) for every H2-measured sample. The paper cites its own earlier work on Pd-decorated DMHCS [33,34] but does not state that the uptake values here were published before, so duplicate_data does not apply. No supplementary file supplied. Research article, not retracted (record flag false; no retraction notice in the PDF).
